function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact numbers myself.  
But you can quickly find out your current download/upload speeds and ping with one of the following methods:

---

### 1. Use an online speed‑test website  
The simplest way is to visit a reputable speed‑test site:

| Site | How to use |
|------|------------|
| **Speedtest.net** (by Ookla) | Go to https://www.speedtest.net/, click “Go” and wait for the test to finish. |
| **Fast.com** (by Netflix) | Visit https://fast.com/ – it automatically starts measuring download speed. |
| **Google Speed Test** | Search “internet speed test” on Google; the built‑in widget will start automatically. |

These sites report:
- **Download speed** (Mbps)
- **Upload speed** (Mbps)
- **Ping / latency** (ms)

---

### 2. Run a command‑line test (if you’re comfortable with the terminal)

#### a. Using `speedtest-cli` (Python package)

If you have Python installed, you can install and run the CLI tool:

```bash
pip install speedtest-cli   # install the package
speedtest-cli --simple      # run a quick test
```

The output will look something like:

```
Host: isp.example.com (123.45.67.89)
Testing download speed........................................
Download: 85.23 Mbit/s
Testing upload speed..........................................
Upload: 12.34 Mbit/s
Ping: 15.6 ms
```

> **Tip:** If you’re on Windows and want to run this directly from the command prompt, you can use the `cmd_controller_execute` tool (see below).

#### b. Using PowerShell’s `Test-NetConnection`

On Windows PowerShell you can run:

```powershell
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName www.google.com -InformationLevel Detailed
```

This will give you latency and packet loss information, though it doesn’t measure throughput.

---

### 3. Using the `cmd_controller_execute` tool (Windows only)

If you’d like me to run a command for you (and you’re on a Windows machine), I can invoke the tool:

```json
{
  "command": "speedtest-cli --simple",
  "unit": "N/A"
}
```

(Just let me know if you want me to try that.)

---

### 4. Check your router’s admin interface

Many modern routers display real‑time bandwidth usage on their status page. Log into your router’s web UI (usually at 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1) and look for a “Status” or “Traffic” tab.

---

### Quick checklist

1. **Open a browser** → go to one of the sites above.  
2. **Run the test** → wait for the results.  
3. **Note the numbers** → compare them to your ISP’s advertised speeds.  

If you’re consistently seeing speeds far below what you’re paying for, you might want to:

- Restart your modem/router.  
- Check for firmware updates.  
- Verify that no other devices are hogging bandwidth.  
- Contact your ISP if the problem persists.

Let me know if you’d like help interpreting the results or troubleshooting specific issues!
